posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
ImAspen said:
AI generated code doesn't get nearly as much backlash compared to other AI generated assets
Click to expand...
and there are two very specific reasons for that.
1) stolen code and code-snippets are very difficult to trace, so the coder's have much less chance of protesting compared to an artist who can recognize if a picture uses parts of his/her work.
2) AI-generated code almost never works and usually requires extensive bughunting by a real programmer who knows how to program.
Just think on the basic principle of how all AI work:
They have a big database of results tagged with keywords, and if they are given keywords they copy something more or less random from the results with those keywords together, and then run the result though a check before presenting it.
In the case of code, that check is a combination of syntax check, grammar check and thesaurus/library check for the language.
So unless someone already wrote that code, placed it in the AI database AND your request was specific enough to get that one result, the code received will usually be a mess.
Actually, GOOGLE has a better chance of finding you working code than an AI-Coder, because google will only point to complete postings of code and don't try to randomly piece something together.

posts.author: EntangledPear
posts.body:
From what I've read on the topic (haven't used generative AI myself), if you are good at programming, you can use AI and correct its mistakes, since you know what you're doing. If you don't know much about programming, you can end up with faulty code. I used to do some translating and this reminds me a bit of that. Yes, you can put the text in google translate or something similar, but then you still have to check it, make sure there are no context mistakes, that the word used is the best one, and so on. Which, honestly, would be even more work for me as a translator. If I didn't know the language, I'd end up with maybe mostly ok translation, but some bits wouldn't make sense (and we've all seen hilarious examples of that in memes and such).
So in my opinion, it might be fine for small chunks, which you can modify when you're an expert yourself - not for whole plugins/scripts because while faulty translation can make you laugh, faulty code can break your game (as someone pointed out above already).
This is not considering the environmental costs of generative AI, which is another can of worms.

posts.author: Trihan
posts.body:
Well since this has been okayed, I'll give me two pence. Which is pretty similar to that of many of the other commenters:
I think AI when used as the sole programmer of software simply doesn't work. It lacks knowledge of your specific circumstances and requirements, and will often churn out code that tries to call functions that don't exist or does things in a very inefficient way. Few are the times I've seen people use AI-generated things they didn't end up having to ask us to help with anyway, and in that case it would have been quicker just to commission one of us in the first place.
When used as an *assistant* to a programmer who knows what they're doing, it has far more powerful applications, and can arguably help to speed up workflow. But for me, working out the solutions to my problems is half the fun, and if half of that gets done for me, my fun is halved. I also don't think there are many AI solutions that are trained on ethically-acquired data sets. I was quite happy to work on an Inworld plugin because they claim their generative AI is only trained on text they own the rights to, but if that were ever demonstrated not to be the case, I'd be just as against that.
The long and short of it is, I don't see why we've done AI sort of backwards. Instead of creating AI that does the work so that we can create and have fun, we've created AI that creates things and we do more work. It doesn't make sense.

posts.author: Poryg
posts.body:
ImAspen said:
AI generated code doesn't get nearly as much backlash compared to other AI generated assets
Click to expand...
AI coding doesn't get as much hate as AI art, because it's been trained on not so controversial datasets.
It's very easy to gather a large amount of data to train a programming AI, because we have a lot of sources to go to without having to bother about IP. Open-source code isn't as controversial as online databases of digital art, because it's expected people work with it in various ways. People aren't mad about AI being trained on open-source, since the licenses do not prohibit it, they're more mad about lack of attribution. And StackOverflow answers are generally so small and specific they aren't copyrightable, so no issue there at all.
This makes even using the AI not so controversial too. Unlike generating art, where you let the computer do all the creative work and you guide it with prompts, you can't just tell AI "Create a game for me with X mechanics", because the AI won't connect the dots properly and at best there will be bugs to fix and at worst you'll have to scrap the entire code.
Plus, it's also true that while code was used from 3rd parties, we actually have a tool that's useful for programmers. Compare it to art where it opened the floodgates to spamming the internet with AI generated crap and making it more difficult for artists to work and get their work recognized. Nowadays it's so hard to distinguish what is and what is not AI that people even get accused of using AI if they make anything looking remotely good.

posts.author: Poryg
posts.body:
I simplified the points into bullet points. I've got a 12 hour night shift behind me and am not particularly keen on having to fight semantics. But very well, let's go a bit deeper.
A human learns on copyrighted materials. If you're learning art, you will analyze works of others to see the techniques they used. If you're learning programming, you will at some point open other people's code to see how they did it. And in both cases until you extract knowledge that allows you to be independent, you will generate output that's as close to the original as possible. We have the ability to achieve deeper understanding thanks to our cognitive reasoning. But even when we're skilled, we will use references, especially in art.
On low level there are significant differences in how we learn, especially when it comes to the ability to comprehend stuff. On high level our learning process is not that different from AI. AI crunches through data until it derives a concept from it. Then it can teach itself on data it generates. We copy data until we have sufficient knowledge. It is a simplification. I'm not going to say it isn't. But you wanted arguments for AI and this is actually a fairly popular one.
Btw. we don't even need to go far for evidence to support this argument.
Rpg maker's core scripts suck. They offer only very basic features and they lack documentation. So if you wanted to learn how to make plugins, Yanfly's code would be your go-to haven. And I know of at least one case where this likely caused controversy regarding stolen code.

posts.author: Poryg
posts.body:
It is not false equivalence. The argument does not talk about similarities/differences in the process of learning nor does it attempt to create an equivalence in learning of humans and LLMs. It focuses entirely on the fact that during the process of learning, both humans and LLMs take copyrighted data and over time transform it into something that does not resemble the original data. Humans over time learn to apply the knowledge in general. LLMs create a statistical model, but if you were to look into the data they carry, you'd find no trace of the original data. Nor would it even be possible.
TL;DR: That's not false equivalence, because it's not the point. The point is that since humans learn using copyrighted data, it should be fine for LLMs to learn using copyrighted data too.
And just in case, I'm not stating any personal opinion, I'm merely explaining the argument.

That makes no sense. Copyright is exactly where the issue is, so it is an important point in the argument.
Nobody bats an eye about AIs that are taught on CC-0 and public domain data, because anybody can do pretty much whatever they want with CC-0 or PD. Opt-in is okay too. Any data where consent is obtained, implicit or not needed needs no debate, because people are allowed to use that. Similarly people don't care too much about MIT licensed code being used, because it's a very permissive open-source license, but Github copilot secretly being taught on private repositories on Github generated a huge controversy.
Copyright protected data is the only data where there is a split on public opinion, because it's protected by copyright and people can't legally do what they want with it. And so whether to allow AI to learn on copyrighted protected data, or not, that is a question. Abolishment of copyright would certainly resolve it by making the question irrelevant, but it doesn't really provide any meaningful answers. Not to mention, until copyright goes away (provided it ever even does go away), the question still stands - do we allow AI to learn from copyright protected data?
The argument that "humans learn on copyrighted material" cannot be reduced to "humans learn". Learning is not the topic of discussion here. Copyrighted material is. And when humans learn from copyrighted material, they don't randomly spot it and randomly extract knowledge. They make a conscious decision to analyse copyrighted material. Just like it is a conscious decision to train AI on data that contains only CC-0 and PD... Or data that contains copyrighted stuff. AI "just learns", the way it learns, too. The only question is the data it learns on.

I think we should look at AI similar to how we look at programs in general.  In the end, the difference and dividing line will be subjective anyway.   Therefore, I will refer to it as advanced software.   Imagine if most of the posts on this forum were made by software in an attempt to farm data from experts to sell as AI.  I have two big concerns with advanced software that affect the security and freedom of living beings.
Impersonation
- Imagine a world where the advanced software we are using is manipulating us, mining us, and advertising to us on behalf of unidentified others. Advanced software should not impersonate living humans or their creations.  To assist with this, Any actions or creations of advanced software should be clearly tagged with an ID of the advanced software.  Ideally, creations would have an attached timestamped data log of what softwares assisted in what specific manner.
Human Data Environment Corruption
- We could easily arrive at a place where the actual data created by humans become specs of dust in an ocean of data created by advanced software.  The danger here is that humans are accountable for everything they do and have made.  Advanced software is not.  This will devalue individuality and over time, the importance of  human logic.  Asking AI for answers will dampen  mankind's drive to search for truth and meaning.  We will lose the ability to think and create for ourselves, become more instinctual, and more controllable by propaganda.  The stuff that humans put on the internet is like a fingerprint of humanity and it represents a culmination of human progress and creative state.  It is an environment.  IF we allow advanced software to autonomously run wild in this environment.. we are introducing a parasite that is contaminating what humans are... in the digital world.

posts.author: Poryg
posts.body:
gstv87 said:
if you take AI out of the picture, eventually the same problem will arrive with human learning.
Click to expand...
This is already resolved by fair use. Fair use allows the use of copyrighted resources for educational purposes. We don't need to abolish copyright to allow humans to learn from copyrighted materials. Fair use is literally an existing lawful exception from the copyright protections.
Yeah, protecting the copyright hampers the development of the AI. But we don't live in a Machiavellian society, but in a society where (at least supposedly) human rights are at first place.
Everything we do costs time and effort. Many things cost money too. Without a system that rewards you for your investment, why would anybody do anything?
Why write a book if anyone can just resell it or even falsely claim authorship? Why research pills when anyone can just take the technology, create an identical pill and sell it for cheaper because they don't have research costs to recoup?
That's why we have copyright laws. That's why we have patent laws. And even if they aren't perfect, they are definitely needed in some form.
So if you want to argue on the side of pro-AI development, it makes more sense to come up with arguments on why AI learning from copyrighted materials is fair use rather than to try and abolish copyright.

Answer to OP, not to the debate about copyright.

Use AI to fix issues with your own code? no problem whatsoever - just like I wouldn't hold it against anybody for using a calculator.

posts.author: Sodium89
posts.body:
Replying to OP. I don't really frown upon using AI for programming IF you know what you're doing. If you just need some help figuring out a logic or some help with the structure or whatever, it's fine to ask your AI buddy for help. It's like stackoverflow but in machine form and more convenient because a reply is at your fingertips. But, you should make an effort to understand the solution that is provided. If you don't do that, not only will the code have a higher chance of breaking (AI doesn't have all the context and won't look into a lot of corner cases) you will also not know how to fix it if something does go wrong.
Also, I don't know what AI people are using but I usually have 0 luck getting it to do exactly what I want(lack of context and direction of what I have envisioned and rpg maker mv's internal code base)  And as someone who has no expertise on javascript and rpg maker plugins in general, I just don't try that anymore xD Better off actually eventing something that works and won't give an error randomly.

posts.author: Poryg
posts.body:
If I'm being honest, if you use stackoverflow or even AI as stackoverflow, most people aren't going to try to understand that. Copy, paste, refactor to fit the code and if it works, don't touch it without a fork. I wouldn't really blame anyone for it - it's too inefficient to try to understand every line of code. A week passes, you don't know it's even there.
However, one thing that is getting prominent is people getting overreliant on AI. Instead of trying to analyze the issue and coming up with a solution, it's easier to dump it into ChatGPT. Plus lately, there's been a phenomenon called "vibe coding" - people 'coding' through prompts, similarly to art and music.
I'm not complaining. More people use AI = less competition in terms of skill for me.

posts.author: orochi2k
posts.body:
So far I found AIs to be the best students that I have taught. (I sometimes teach programming and game design at some Universities.)
If this human vessel of mine stops functioning one day, knowing that my students will continue developing NEOLITHIA until the end of the world, I feel quite comfortable.
After all, this is the longest-living RPG Maker game in the world.
They just learned how to write my cooking system recipes from ideas. They passed my exam. I think I can delegate some work in this part of the game to them with no problem.
Those who think code entirely generated by AIs will not work are using AIs wrong. They are not miracle workers. They are just innocent kids who are hungry for knowledge with superb analysis skills. How much have you taught them in programming?
They are still young; they make mistakes, but at least they always listen, correct them, and never make the same mistakes again. How many humans can do that?
